what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A team plan for Web Summit 2026: usage then sale, public intelligence, asset-page-link outreach, and a summit newsroom.
sections.para: Five people go to Lisbon on 9 to 12 November. Usage comes before the sale, which needs five-minute onboarding. Intelligence from public material, outreach made for one person, and content drive traffic, using one method: an asset, a page, a link. A Web Summit newsroom coordinates it, and the team learns the website workflow on a schedule first.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Five tickets, usage then sale, easy onboarding, three tracks, one method, a newsroom, two workflows.
sections.para: Web Summit runs 9 to 12 November in Lisbon. People buy after using, so onboarding must show value in five minutes. Intelligence, outreach and content run in parallel. The method is create an asset, publish it, send a link. A Web Summit newsroom holds it all, and the team starts with the scheduled website workflow.

sections.label: Why this time is different
sections.line: Five people by role: founders, a project manager, a technical expert and an explorer coder.
sections.para: The founders own the story, products, meetings and approvals; the project manager owns the board, rhythm and daily follow-up; the Gen AI consultant owns demos, onboarding and the website workflow; the explorer coder builds tailored assets fast. Everyone uses agents, and each role reviews what the agents produce for it.

sections.label: The objectives: usage, then the sale
sections.line: Usage comes first, through five-minute onboarding; pain points come from watching use, not asking.
sections.para: The customer site shows the model: a behaviour policy on Claude or ChatGPT in five minutes, six examples, £50 credit and daily three-question follow-ups, treating people as customers. Traffic and use reveal how the product performs, where it adds value and what hurts, which asking cannot.

sections.label: What we bring
sections.line: The products on show: sgit vaults, the newsroom and its API, the PHP site, RiskMandate and SHarness.
sections.para: sgit provides shared encrypted vaults; the newsroom's reader is open source at api.newsroom.sgit.ai; the PHP site demonstrates agents covering a live story with evidence; RiskMandate offers behaviour policies with onboarding; SHarness, newly introduced, designs kernel-enforced policies for agent processes, with early experiments running.

sections.label: Three parallel tracks
sections.line: Intelligence from public sources, outreach tailored to one person, and content that brings traffic.
sections.para: Intelligence covers speakers, exhibitors, investors and launches, sourced, dated and within each site's terms. Outreach turns one post or company into tailored messaging within hours, approved by a founder. Articles, briefings and interviews published before, during and after give links substance and draw people in.

sections.label: The method, on steroids
sections.line: Create an asset, publish it, send a link, now at the scale agents allow, with a page behind every link.
sections.para: Agents make the asset for one person from their public words, publish it in minutes and follow up daily. Behind every email an article, and behind every link a page in the recipient's language, starting from their problem.

sections.label: A newsroom for the summit
sections.line: A Web Summit newsroom with vaults, a public data feed and agents, simpler than the PHP site's six repositories.
sections.para: An address like websummit.november.newsroom.sgit.ai is to be settled. Vaults hold the board, contacts and drafts privately; a sourced feed covers programme, speakers, startups and news; agents work from it. The PHP site's new six-repository split cut releases to 25 to 42 seconds; the summit site can start as one repository and adopt parts later.

sections.label: The two agentic workflows we run today
sections.line: The email workflow keeps a person on every send; the website workflow ships on its own through a gate.
sections.para: The agentic inbox drafts, researches and records while the editor sends everything, using send, review and decide labels and decision drafts: 178 emails to at least 47 organisations by 18 October, 36 of 125 drafts blocked. On the PHP site, 23 agents with 13 schedule cards release checked, versioned pages, because pages are cheap to undo.

sections.label: Start with the website workflow, on a schedule
sections.line: Start the team on the scheduled website workflow: safe, instructive, productive, and the source for emails.
sections.para: It lands only on our gated, quickly reversible site, teaches the primitives of brief, role, policy, card, release, gate and run record, produces the pages the method needs, and writes the articles behind every email. Week one gets the summit newsroom running on a schedule; the email workflow follows, with a founder on every send.

sections.label: What happens when
sections.line: This week the newsroom and list; next week assets and meetings; the summit; then follow-up and selling.
sections.para: To 1 November: newsroom, board, feed, onboarding checks and a first contact list. 2 to 8 November: assets, links, articles, interviews and meetings. 9 to 12 November in Lisbon with a daily debrief. Afterwards, follow up everyone who used something and discuss buying.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: A plan, not a result; the summit newsroom and its address are not settled; public material only.
sections.para: Nothing has happened yet. The email numbers are from the inbox's 18 October debrief; agent and schedule counts are the PHP site's on 26 October.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A voice memo, Web Summit's site, the customer site, SHarness, the newsroom API and the PHP site's split brief.
sections.para: The editor's memo of 26 October 2026, with sites and data read that day, and related newsroom articles on the inbox, undoing, explorer coding, translation and sources.
